text: REST, SOAP, and event-driven integration are the three protocol styles behind the patterns from the last lesson. Each one shows up constantly in real ServiceNow integration work.

REST organizes itself around resources, each addressed by a URL, acted on with standard HTTP verbs — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE — and the payload is almost always JSON. It's simple, self-explanatory, and easy to debug, which is exactly why it's the modern default and what course six's Scripted REST APIs were built on.

SOAP predates REST's dominance and takes a stricter approach. Every SOAP service is described by a WSDL contract spelling out exactly which operations exist and what shape each request and response takes. The body is always XML — more verbose, but self-describing.

That rigidity is exactly why SOAP is still alive. Regulated, slow-moving industries like finance, government, and telecom often run core systems fifteen or twenty years old that were never rewritten for REST. If you integrate with a bank's ledger or a government records system, SOAP may be the only interface available, and ServiceNow supports it specifically for this reason.

Both REST and SOAP, in their typical form, are request-response: something asks, something answers, right now. Event-driven integration pushes a notification the instant something happens, through a webhook or a message queue, instead of either side polling on a loop asking if anything changed.

The monitoring-tool example from Lesson one is event-driven: the tool doesn't wait to be asked, it pushes the moment it detects a problem. It usually still rides on HTTP, so it's a separate category by behavior — who initiates and when — not by JSON versus XML.

The external system's existing architecture decides which pattern you use, not your preference. A developer who only knows REST will eventually hit a legacy SOAP system and get stuck — which is why all three matter before any hands-on building begins.
